result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.difference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Compute the difference of this graph and another graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.difference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Compute the difference of this graph and another graph. title: >- [Graph.difference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute the difference of this graph and another graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the difference of this graph and another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L39239-L39346){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.difference(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Difference](../assets/graphs/difference.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G has edges A–B, B–D, and A–C; H has A–B, B–D, and C–D. G minus H keeps only A–C (accent), the one edge of G that H lacks. The shared edges A–B and B–D are dashed, and nodes B and D, left with no edges, are dropped." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing edges that are in this graph but not in the other graph. Nodes are included if they are endpoints of remaining edges. Edges are matched by their endpoint node IDs: an edge of this graph is removed when `other` connects the same pair of IDs (in the same direction, for directed graphs), regardless of weights or attributes. Difference answers "what does this graph have that the other one does not?", which is useful for: - finding connections that appeared (or disappeared) between two snapshots - removing a known set of edges, such as a background or reference network, to see what is specific to this one - checking which predicted links are not yet in an observed network Nodes are matched by ID, so both graphs must use the same numbering for the same entities. Nodes that are not endpoints of a remaining edge are dropped, including nodes that were isolated in this graph. All remaining nodes and edges keep this graph's labels, attributes, weights and edge IDs; `other` contributes nothing but its edge set. Neither input graph is modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to subtract. It must have the same directedness as this graph. Only its edges (as pairs of node IDs) matter; its nodes, labels, attributes, and weights are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing edges in this graph but not in `other`, plus their endpoints. It is weighted if this graph is weighted. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Difference returns edges in the calling graph that are absent from `other`, and suppresses any node that becomes edge-isolated as a result. It is asymmetric: `g1.difference(g2)` and `g2.difference(g1)` capture different sides of what changed, which is why change-detection workflows typically call both. Both operands must have the same directedness. Node and edge attributes come from the calling graph. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Only edge `3-4` is unique to the first graph, so that's the only one that survives: ::: {#039c44bb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Original network g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 5): g1.add_node() g1.add_edges([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]) # Subset network g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): g2.add_node() g2.add_edges([(1, 2), (2, 3)]) diff = g1.difference(g2) diff.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: Only the endpoints of that edge remain as nodes; nodes `1` and `2` are dropped: ::: {#8c773150 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} diff.get_node_ids() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [3, 4] ``` ::: ::: This asymmetry is what makes `difference()` useful for detecting change over time. With two yearly snapshots of a friendship network (built with the same people in the same order, so IDs match), `year1.difference(year2)` surfaces the friendship that ended: ::: {#ff845a76 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def snapshot(friendships): g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cat", "Dan", "Eve"]) g.add_edges(friendships) return g year1 = snapshot([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Cat", "Dan"), ("Dan", "Eve")]) year2 = snapshot([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Ann", "Cat"), ("Dan", "Eve")]) year1.difference(year2).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Cat--Dan'] ``` ::: ::: Swapping the order surfaces the friendship that was formed instead: ::: {#d7c14a3a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} year2.difference(year1).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['Ann--Cat'] ``` ::: :::
